newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FORECAST - Ayala 6-mo net seen marginally up.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Ayala 6-mo net seen marginally up.

text.p: The Philippines' largest conglomerate Ayala Corp should post a small rise in first-half profits with property remaining its mainstay despite recent fears over the sector, analysts said.

A Reuters survey of six Manila brokerages, completed on Wednesday, showed analysts expecting an average a four percent rise in net profit to 3.59 billion pesos, up from 3.45 billion in the six months ended June 30, 1996.
Most analysts were maintaining their predictions for full year 1997 earnings for the flagship of a group that traces its roots to a distillery set up in Manila in 1834.
But one analyst differed saying he had downgraded his forecasts since the beginning of the year.
"This company depends for nearly half of its revenue on the property sector and that is going down," he said.
About 40 percent of its revenue comes from Ayala Land which owns prime properties in the country's foremost business district, Makati.
An equal amount comes from Bank of the Philippine Islands, which was strengthened last year by a merger with a smaller bank, Citytrust Banking Corp.
Last month, a scare that real estate prices were set to crash took the shine off property firms as well as banks on fears they were over-exposed to the sector.
The fears have since died down. On Wednesday, property stocks were leading a minor rally on the Philippine bourse with Ayala Land gaining 3.5 percent to 22.25 pesos in early trade.
"Ayala Land has a pretty good mix of property," Spencer Yap, analyst at BPI Capital Corp, said, adding that fears of overheating were restricted to the upper end of the market.
Anscor Hagedorn Securities research head Noel Reyes said the company's prestigious "Ayala Triangle" complex, which houses the Makati trading floor of the Philippine Stock Exchange, had done well.
"Even if they have sold half of it (Ayala Triangle), then it is good enough," Reyes said.
The perceived loan quality problems would not affect Bank of the Philippine Islands because it has always been a conservative bank, Giovanni dela Rosa, analyst at ING Barings said.
The poll yielded a relatively wide variation in the forecasts for Ayala Corp's full year 1997 profits with the top at eight billion pesos and the lowest at 5.7 billion.
The average numbers predicted a profit of 7.03 billion pesos, up 12.84 percent over last year.

The family-controlled Ayala Corp, whose president Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala descends from Spanish landowners who settled in the Philippines, also has interests in food, telecommunications, insurance and electronic components.
Its mobile phone firm Globe Telecom has been hit by fraudulent calls and one analyst estimated it could lose about 300 million pesos this year.
Ayala Life Assurance would post modest profits while Pure Foods Corp was recovering from last year's high material costs and a poultry glut, analysts said.
Integrated Microelectronics Inc, although contributing a small portion of the conglomerate's profits, was growing rapidly.
Recently, the company entered a $600 million railway project in the Philippines and won a 25-year concession to run Manila's waterworks and sewerage system.
